'''Kenneth Eric Money''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|MSC}} (January 4, 1935 – March 6, 2023) was a Canadian scientist specializing in the human ear and an Olympic [[high jumper]]. He worked at the [[Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine]] in Toronto. He published over one hundred science articles and authored six different topics in the ''[[World Book Encyclopedia]]''.

==Education==
Money attended [[North Toronto Collegiate Institute]] for high school. He then enrolled at the [[University of Toronto]] and earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[physiology]] and [[chemistry]] in 1958, a [[Master of Science]] in physiology in 1959, and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physiology in 1961.

==Sports==
In 1956, Money competed in the [[1956 Summer Olympics|Olympic Games]] and placed fifth in the high jump.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Wallechinsky|first1=David|authorlink1=David Wallechinsky|last2=Loucky|first2=Jaime|year=2012|title=The Complete Book of the Olympics 2012 Edition|page=211|location=[[London]]|publisher=[[Aurum Press]]|isbn=978-1-84513-695-6}}</ref> His personal best in this event was 2.03 m.<ref>[https://www.olympedia.org/athletes/66179 Ken Money]. olympedia.org</ref>

==Research==
Some of his contributions in the scientific field include knowledge of the inner ear, [[motion sickness]], [[disorientation]], and biological effects of space flight. Other of Money's interests included [[badminton]], [[skiing]], [[acrobatic flying]], [[skydiving]], [[fishing]], and reading.

Money was selected by the [[National Research Council of Canada]] as an astronaut candidate in December 1983, but left the [[Canadian Astronaut Corps]] in 1992 without having flown in space.  He acted as [[Spacelab]] Payload Operations Controller for a Spacelab mission in 1992. During the same mission, Money served as the alternate astronaut, having the capability to fly if needed.

Money is credited with the invention of an experimental surgical operation called [[semicircular canal]] plugging,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Semeniuk |first1=Ivan |title=Physiologist Ken Money was one of Canada’s original group of six astronauts |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-physiologist-ken-money-was-one-of-canadas-original-group-of-six/ |website=The Globe and Mail |access-date=20 December 2024 |date=12 March 2023 |quote=Money also developed a surgical procedure, known as semicircular canal plugging, that can be used to treat a particular form of dizziness.}}</ref> which is now being used in North America and Europe to treat particular types of dizzy spells. He also worked part-time as a professor of physiology for the [[University of Toronto]] and regularly lectured to undergraduate classes.

==Personal life and death==
Ken Money had a brother Bill, who predeceased him. Ken died at the Sunnybrook Veterans Centre in Toronto, on March 6, 2023. He was 88, and he was survived by his wife Sheila Money (née Donnelly). They married around 1958 and had a daughter Laura and three grandchildren.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kenneth Eric Money |url=https://www.legacy.com/ca/obituaries/theglobeandmail/name/kenneth-money-obituary?id=49650839 |website=Legacy |access-date=8 March 2023}}</ref>

==Awards and service==
In 1994, he was awarded the [[Meritorious Service Cross]] by the [[Governor General of Canada]] for his many contributions to science and technology.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mr. Kenneth Money |url=https://www.gg.ca/en/honours/recipients/136-10774 |website=[[Governor General of Canada]] |access-date=8 March 2023}}</ref>

Money was also a member of the volunteer [[Board of Governors]] of the [[National Space Society]], a [[non-profit]] [[space advocacy]] group founded by [[Wernher von Braun]].
